issues.title: Seam: Earnings Radar and Sector Rotation import each other (MACRO_SERIES / macro_weekly_closes)
issues.summary: Earnings Radar and Sector Rotation import each other for MACRO_SERIES and macro_weekly_closes, so neither board can be read or changed on its own.

detail.whats_wrong:
Area: `earnings` / `market`.
From the misplaced-seams table of `docs/system_map.md` (Structure A, `#24`). Listed there, filed here; **not reviewed** — do not build from this issue alone.

The two areas import each other:

- `module_earnings_radar/macro_watch.py:16` — `from RevenueChaser.module_sector_rotation.universe import MACRO_SERIES` (used at `:123`)
- `module_sector_rotation/engine.py:550` — `from RevenueChaser.module_earnings_radar.macro_watch import macro_weekly_closes`

The second one is written inside a function rather than at module top level, which is how the cycle is currently survived. `module_earnings_radar/report.py:1578` is a third reader of the same file, also lazily.
detail.evidence: A mutual import between two board areas is the one shape that cannot be reasoned about locally: either module's top-level import order can break the other, and the workaround (function-level imports) hides it from the reader instead of removing it. This is the FRED/rotation seam, and it has already forced two lazy imports.
detail.example: `module_sector_rotation/engine.py:550` imports `macro_weekly_closes` inside a function and `module_earnings_radar/report.py:1578` does the same: move either import to module top level and the other module stops importing. That is the test the fix has to pass, and it is why the cycle is invisible to a reader of either file.
detail.tried_or_decided: PARKED until after Sunday 25 Oct (owner, 2026-10-22). Filed from the Structure A seam table of `docs/system_map.md` (#24) and not reviewed, so nothing here is approved to build. The two halves were split at filing time because they can land independently.
detail.direction:
Two halves, and they are independent:
1. `MACRO_SERIES` moves out of the board module with `ROTATION_ETFS` (see the companion `ROTATION_ETFS` issue), which removes the earnings → rotation half.
2. `macro_weekly_closes` is a weekly-closes reader over stored macro series; deciding whether it belongs to `earnings` at all, or to a shared macro reader both areas import, removes the rotation → earnings half. Whichever way it goes, the top-level import must then be legal — the test is that neither module needs a function-level import of the other.

issues.title: Theme labels: the offline label of a merged theme depends on tag-table row order when groups tie (deferred until after Sunday)
issues.summary: A merged theme's offline label depends on tag-table row order when two groups tie, so the same data can produce different labels across runs.

detail.whats_wrong:
STATUS 2026-10-22: OPEN, DEFERRED until after Sunday 25 Oct (found while fixing a CI failure of #51; logged, not built).

`relabel_from_tags` (`module_relatedness/themes.py:393-430`) builds a medium theme's offline label from the tags of its member fine themes: `med_tags.setdefault(parent, []).extend(ordered)` for each fine theme, then `_label(Counter(tags).most_common(), ...)`. The fine themes are visited in the order of `fine_tags`, which is filled from `run_rows("relatedness_theme_tags", run_id)`, a read with NO `ORDER BY`. When two merged fine themes have equal size and equal tag counts, `Counter.most_common()` keeps first-seen order, so the label is whichever group's tag rows the scan returns first.
detail.evidence: Small: it is the OFFLINE fallback label (LLM naming replaces it) and only on exact ties, but a label that differs between machines makes comparisons and snapshots of runs unreliable.
detail.example: The #51 e2e (`module_testing/e2e/test_board_relatedness.py::test_board_renders_after_a_rebuild`) seeds three equal groups (semiconductors G, banks B, healthcare H, 30 profiles each). The medium cut merges the bank and healthcare fine themes. On Windows the merged theme was labelled `branch, consumer, deposits` (banks), on the hosted Linux CI run `biologics, clinical, drugs` (healthcare). Same data, same code, a different label. The test now accepts either (commit 96fb3dd on `area/classification/433-theme-naming-fix`); the engine was left alone.
detail.direction: Make the order deterministic: iterate `sorted(fine_tags.items())` (or read the tag table with `ORDER BY theme_id, rank`). Note it can change the label of tied merged themes on already stored runs, so decide whether stored labels are rewritten or only new runs follow the rule.
detail.next_step: Deliberately left for after Sunday 25 Oct. Decide the tie-break with #51, which is the same naming code, then fix both in one commit.

detail.evidence:
Reproduced on clean `main` `a60bbb2` in a detached worktree with no local changes, and at the same point on a branch that touches `core/identity/refresh.py`, so no branch is the cause. It is the same class as the known crash in `module_settings/tests/test_inventory*.py` that CLAUDE.md already leaves to CI, with a wider scope.

1. Narrow it: run the directory with `-p no:randomly` and `-x` per file to find the test that kills the process, then bisect its fixtures. The crash lands well into the run, so a shared resource released twice is likelier than any single assertion.
2. Suspect the native extensions: DuckDB connection handling in the store fixtures (closed twice, or used after close across teardown) and anything holding a C-level handle across a `monkeypatch` teardown.
3. If one fixture is at fault, fix it; if it is an interpreter or driver interaction, mark the directory as a CI-only tier the way the inventory tests are, and say so in CLAUDE.md so the rule and the reality agree.

issues.title: Run log: a job_runs row can stay "running" for ever when the end write is skipped
issues.summary: A dashboard job whose end write loses the store keeps a job_runs row saying "running" for ever, and nothing reconciles it after a restart.

detail.whats_wrong: `app/jobs._record` (`app/jobs.py:258-276`) is the only writer of a dashboard job's `job_runs` row and upserts it twice, at start and at end. The end write is wrapped in `rawstore.brief_wait()`, so a job whose end write loses the store to another process keeps a row that says `running` with `finished_at` NULL. Nothing reconciles it: the in-memory registry is cleared on restart (`:16-17`), there is no sweeper, and `pid` (`:270`) is recorded but never checked again. The scheduled writer has the same shape (`core/automations.py:839-841`).
detail.evidence: A 13F ingest holds `raw.duckdb` in chunks (`module_sec_13f/engine.py:530`). A universe job finishing while a chunk holds the file exceeds `brief_wait`, its end write is skipped and logged as `job_runs: could not record job <id>`, and the run log shows that run as `running` even after a restart. Nothing reads `job_runs` yet, so it is invisible today; it stops being invisible the moment PL5-b adds the reader the table was built for (#282 J4), and a run log that lies about what is running is worse than no run log.
detail.example:
A 13F ingest holds `raw.duckdb` in chunks (`module_sec_13f/engine.py:530`). The universe job finishes while one of
those chunks holds the file; its end write exceeds `brief_wait`, is skipped and logged as
`job_runs: could not record job <id>`. The run log now shows that universe run as `running`. The dashboard is
restarted that evening. The row still says `running`, and the first reader of the table (PL5-b, or Data Health)
will show a run that has been going for days.
detail.direction:
1. A sweep at startup, the cheapest fix: on the dashboard's first store call, mark every `running` row whose `pid` is not alive as `error` with a message saying the dashboard restarted while it ran. `core/procs.pid_alive` exists and `core/job_lock` already makes that judgement; a reused PID needs the start-time check in `core/job_lock._holder_live` (`core/job_lock.py:152-164`), or accept the looser answer and say so.
2. A fallback log file for the skipped write, as the 2026-10-02 review of #124 suggested: append the end record under `.cache/logs/` when the store write is skipped and replay it on the next successful write.
detail.next_step: Build it with the rest of PL5-b, starting with the startup sweep and a test that a stale `running` row from a dead pid becomes `error`.

issues.title: Run log: the dashboard writer leaves job_runs.trigger, source, registry_name and counts NULL
issues.summary: The dashboard writer leaves job_runs.trigger, source, registry_name and counts NULL, so the column meant to say where a run came from is empty for every human-started run.

detail.whats_wrong: `job_runs` declares sixteen columns (`core/rawstore.py:1491-1503`) and the two writers fill different subsets. The scheduler (`core/automations.py:829-841`, #129 A1) sets `trigger` to `"scheduled"` and fills `registry_name`; the dashboard (`app/jobs.py:268-274`) leaves `trigger`, `source`, `registry_name` and `counts` NULL. The 2026-10-02 review of #124 asked for a source column to tell a CLI run from a dashboard run; the columns arrived with #282 and the dashboard writer never filled them.
detail.evidence: Read last night's run log and two `daily_bars` rows come back: one from `RC-Daily-Bars` with `trigger = "scheduled"` and `registry_name = "RC-Daily-Bars"`, and one from a Fetch someone pressed with `trigger = NULL`. "NULL means a person pressed it" is a rule nobody can see in the data, and a hand-run CLI would be indistinguishable from the second. `counts` is the same gap from the other side: a job that wrote 4,251 rows reports it only in the prose of `message`, so the log cannot be grouped or summed.
detail.example:
Read the run log for last night and you get two `daily_bars` rows: one from `RC-Daily-Bars` with
`trigger = "scheduled"`, `registry_name = "RC-Daily-Bars"`, and one from a Fetch someone pressed afterwards with
`trigger = NULL`. "NULL means a person pressed it" is a rule nobody can see in the data, and a third writer
(a hand-run CLI) would be indistinguishable from the second.

`counts` is the same kind of gap from the other side: a job that wrote 4,251 rows reports that only in the prose of
`message`, so the run log cannot be grouped or summed by anything.
detail.direction:
1. `app/jobs._record` sets `trigger = "dashboard"` and `source` to the pid or the lane; pick one and write it in the column comment. One dict literal, one test.
2. `registry_name` stays NULL for a dashboard job, which is correct because there is no registry entry; say so in the MANIFEST comment so the next reader does not read it as an omission.

issues.title: job_lock.acquire(wait>0) crashes the process on Windows inside pytest
issues.summary: job_lock.acquire with a positive wait dies with a Windows access violation inside pytest instead of waiting, so the waiting branch cannot be tested or used.

detail.whats_wrong: `core/job_lock.acquire(name, wait=N)` with `N > 0`, called while the lock is held, dies in its retry loop instead of returning: `Windows fatal exception: access violation` at `core/job_lock.py:305` (`os.close(fd)`), after which the test process hangs until it is killed. detail.evidence: The same call outside pytest behaves correctly and returns after its full wait (measured 30.2 s for `wait=30`), so it looks like a host or Python 3.14 interaction with the retry loop rather than a logic error in the lock. No production caller waits: every `acquire()` in the tree passes `wait=0`, verified across the repo. The waiting branch is dead code today, but the crash already cost a mutation check in PL6-a (#26) - turning one `wait=0` into `wait=15` cannot be proven while the process dies instead of waiting, and a substitute mutation covered the slice.
detail.direction: Narrow it before changing anything: run the retry loop under pytest with `faulthandler` on and confirm whether the fault is `os.close(fd)` on a descriptor the failed `msvcrt.locking` attempt already invalidated. If so, do not close a descriptor the attempt did not take, and re-open per attempt. Keep `wait=0` everywhere until it is fixed, and mark a test that needs the waiting path as skipped on Windows rather than leaving it to hang.

issues.title: LEAPS: raw exception text reaches the board notice and the recorded run, so a store error puts a filesystem path on the board
issues.summary: LEAPS puts the full exception text, including a file path, into the board notice and the recorded run when a store read fails; the same shape appears three more times.

detail.whats_wrong: module_leaps/scan.py:78 builds a warning with the exception's full str(); app/runners.py:384 shows it as the board notice and :388 stores it in the result history. A locked or unreadable DuckDB file puts an absolute host path on the board.
detail.evidence: Found in the review of PR #99. The full text is already in the logger.warning on the line above; the same pattern is at module_leaps/engine.py:525 and two more sites.
detail.direction:
**Recommended: put only `type(e).__name__` in the sentence that is shown or stored**, and leave the full text to the logger. The sentence's job is to tell the reader that baselines are missing and that a Quiet label there means missing history; the exception's class is enough to tell a lock from a corrupt file, and anything more belongs in the log.

**Why `redact` is not the answer on its own.** The project does scrub persisted exception text elsewhere — `core/identity/refresh.py:206` and `:213` wrap it as `redact(f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")[:500]` — but `redact` (`core/identity/sources/__init__.py:73`) removes **configured API key values and bearer tokens**, not file paths. detail.whats_wrong:
The root `conftest.py` redirects the data roots away from the developer's real tree — `RC_STORE_DIR`, `RC_CACHE_DIR`, `RC_EDGAR_DOCS_DIR`, `RC_DISCORD_MEDIA_DIR`, `SPX_GAMMA_DATA_ROOT` at `conftest.py:22-45`. Only the store got per-test isolation: `isolate_rawstore` (`conftest.py:130-131`) is autouse and explicitly "Kept **per-test** (never per-session)". **The board artifacts got the root, not the isolation.**

So a test that renders or saves a board payload leaves it in a directory the next test reads. A Refresh test that does not redirect the artifact constants itself reads […]
detail.evidence: Found in the review of PR #102: its first witness test passed for exactly this reason, from a leftover saved payload, and was only caught because the witness had to fail first. conftest.py:22-45 redirects the roots once per worker; only the store is isolated per test (conftest.py:130-131).
detail.direction:
An **autouse fixture that points the per-board artifact constants at `tmp_path`** — the same move the conftest already made for the store, one level finer. Doing it this way means a test that forgets to isolate gets isolation anyway, which is exactly the argument `isolate_rawstore`'s docstring already makes for the store.
detail.next_step: After Sunday 25 Oct 2026: give each test its own artifact root in conftest.py (tmp_path per test) so Refresh tests cannot read an earlier Fetch, then remove the per-test monkeypatch workarounds.

detail.whats_wrong: datetime is a subclass of date, so isinstance(value, date) lets a datetime through and its isoformat() carries a time part. detail.evidence: Found in the review of PR #112; core/tests/test_ledger.py:121-122 already asserts type(x) is date, the exact-type form.
detail.direction:
Use the exact-type check, `type(value) is date`, wherever the intent is "a plain session date and not a timestamp" — or route the value through `core/calendar.to_session_date` and fix the check **inside** that helper, so there is one place that decides. A `datetime` that does arrive should become `value.date()` rather than `None`, where that is what the caller means — worth deciding per call site rather than globally, since `to_session_date` returning `None` for a timestamp may be the honest answer for a stored key.

issues.summary: A new issue lands in the registry with scope board and empty boards, which matches no dashboard, so it is invisible until someone fills the boards by hand.

detail.whats_wrong:
A label is not what puts an issue on a board. The panel lists an entry under "This board" only when the entry's
scope is `board` **and** the board's key is in its `boards` list:

- `core/open_issues.py:238` — `if entry.scope == "board" and board_key in entry.boards`
- `core/open_issues.py:7-11` — the three scopes: `board` ("This board"), `shared` ("Affects every board", on
  every data board), `repo` ("Repository-wide", on Settings / Data health only)

And `boards` is **curated by hand**, never derived from the `area:*` labels:

- `scripts/open_issues_sync.py:8-9` — the curated keys "are never overwritten"
- `scripts/open_issues_sync.py:238` — a newly synced issue is added with `"boards": []`, `scope: "board"`,
  `status: "open"`

`scope: "board"` with an empty `boards` list is the one combination that matches no board. So **every issue the
sync adds is invisible on every panel […]
detail.evidence: core/open_issues.py:238 lists an entry under This board only when scope is board and the board key is in boards; scripts/open_issues_sync.py:238 adds new issues with boards [] and status open, and never overwrites curated keys.
detail.direction:
Two separate things, and only the second is a code change:

1. **The data.** The registry-refresh PR runs `scripts/open_issues_sync.py --write`, drops the closed nine, adds
   the fifteen with their `boards` filled, and fixes the five stale statuses. The board map to apply is
   `/mnt/project-files/plans/2026-10-23_undecided_work/registry_map.txt`.
2. **The gap that let it happen.** Either `open_issues_sync.py` seeds `boards` from the `area:*` labels on a new
   entry (a mapping table, area → board keys, with the multi-board areas left for a human), or `--report-thin`
   grows a check that names every `scope: "board"` entry with no boards, so the drift is reported instead of
   silent. The second is smaller and cannot guess wrong.
detail.next_step: After Sunday 25 Oct 2026: make the sync derive boards from the area labels (or refuse to write an entry that matches no board) and add a test; until then every sync round needs the hand-filled boards of this registry refresh.
